title: BRFL: A Blockchain-based Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning Model

C-a.quote: we propose the Blockchain-based Federated Learning model (BRFL), which contains two main components: the Proof of Pearson Correlation Coefficient consensus algorithm (PPCC) and the Precision-based Spectral Aggregation (PSA) algorithm.
C-a.locator: §I; each component's purpose is stated in the paper's own contribution list -- PPCC at contribution 2, "The algorithm selects the node with the highest Pearson correlation coefficient between the previous round's local model and the global model as the aggregation node. This approach enhances the security of federated learning and resolves the problem of lacking test data in FL", and PSA at §I, "PSA clusters local models with high correlation and verifies their accuracy by calculating the average value, thereby detecting malicious models". Within PSA the two operations are themselves two of the three defense families the paper's own related work enumerates (§II: lp distance-based, cosine angle-based, accuracy validation-based)

C-b.quote: However, individually verifying the accuracy of each local model can consume a significant amount of computational resources of the aggregation nodes (AN ). Moreover, the computational capacity of the AN limits the application of such schemes ... Therefore, after clustering the local models, we only verify the accuracy of the cluster average model gradient denoted CL as ACCa;λ
C-b.locator: §IV (PSA); the same reason is given for the whole design at §I, where the three families' individual deficiencies are listed -- "The lp distance-based method can be vulnerable to attackers who add little biases ... In the cosine angle-based method, attackers can manipulate the angles ... As for the accuracy validation-based method, it requires an additional test dataset and significant computational resources" -- followed by "To address these issues, we propose the Blockchain-based Federated Learning model (BRFL), which contains two main components"

C-c.quote: Experiments conducted on two commonly used datasets demonstrate that our aggregation algorithm surpasses both classic and state-of-the-art baseline methods in terms of accuracy.
C-c.locator: §I contribution 4; the evidence is §V-E's Figure 3, "Figure 3a illustrates the accuracy comparison between our proposed PSA and the baselines when using the MNIST dataset with IID data distribution and noise attack as the model poison attack. From Figure 3a, we observe that our PSA achieves the highest accuracy among all the algorithms", with the malicious fraction set to 50%

C-d.quote: Additionally, we set the number of malicious clients to be half of the total number of local training clients.
C-d.locator: §V-E; the complete set of axes in §V-E is the dataset (MNIST / Fashion-MNIST), the data distribution (IID / non-IID), the attack (noise / sign-flipping) and the competing aggregator (Krum, median, mean, clipped clustering). Num_cluster, the spectral clustering's cluster count, appears only as an algorithm input in Algorithm 2 and is never varied; no variant of BRFL with a stage removed, substituted or re-parameterized appears anywhere in the paper

C-e.quote: This algorithm verifies the accuracy of the average gradient within each cluster using the aggregation nodes’ local datasets, selects the average gradient from the cluster with higher accuracy as the global model. This approach ensures that the global model maintains high accuracy even in the presence of a high percentage of malicious models.
C-e.locator: §I contribution 3; the composition-level version is at §V-F, "This is because in the BRFL model, malicious models are detected, and malicious nodes are prevented from becoming aggregation nodes", which attributes an observed outcome to the two components jointly

coder_note:
THIS IS THE SECOND PRIMARY = YES, AND IT ARRIVED IN THE SAME BATCH AS THE FIRST. Twenty papers are coded; Fedward (2307.00356) and BRFL are the only two with C-a and C-b and C-c and C-e and no identifying contrast. The two are independent of each other -- different venues, different years, different mechanism families, no citation between them -- so the co-occurrence is not one lineage.

WHY C-a = YES ON TWO INDEPENDENT GROUNDS. At the model level, PPCC and PSA are the paper's own "two main components", applied in sequence within a round, and each carries a stated defense purpose in the contribution list: PPCC keeps malicious nodes out of the aggregator role ("enhances the security of federated learning", and §V-F states the effect, "malicious nodes are prevented from becoming aggregation nodes"), PSA detects malicious models. At the stage level, PSA is itself a composition of two of the three defense families the paper's OWN related work separates: correlation-based clustering and accuracy validation. That second grounding is the stronger one, because the taxonomy is the paper's, not the coder's. Amendment 3 is engaged only to note what does NOT count: the blockchain layer's stated purposes are traceability, incentives and storage ("This integration enables traceability of malicious models and provides incentives for locally trained clients"), so it is not a third defense component, and the C-a code does not rest on it.

C-b IS THE CLEANEST PAIRING REASON IN THE FRAME SO FAR, AND IT IS A REASON OF A KIND THE PRE-REGISTRATION DID NOT ANTICIPATE. C-b's frozen text offers two admissible reasons -- constituents individually effective, or complementary threat coverage. BRFL's reason is neither exactly: clustering is paired with accuracy validation because accuracy validation ALONE IS TOO EXPENSIVE, and clustering reduces the number of validations from one per client to one per cluster. That is a pairing chosen by a constituent's property (its cost), and it satisfies C-b's operative requirement that the quotation show the reason for pairing rather than merely that a pairing exists. The complementary-coverage reading is available too and is quoted in the locator: §I lists a distinct failure mode for each of the three families and then proposes the composition "To address these issues". Recorded here because A5's prose should say that pairing reasons in this literature include cost complementarity, not only threat complementarity.

WHY C-d = NO SURVIVES RULE 4. Rule 4 gives the benefit of the doubt to "any experiment plausibly holding a downstream mechanism fixed while varying an upstream stage", and there is no candidate. §V-E's four axes are all external. The four "This is because" explanations in §V-F and §V-G are genuine mechanism reasoning, but every one of them explains a BLOCKCHAIN measurement -- the size of the chain a node stores, how often a node is selected to aggregate -- not the defense outcome, and none is produced by varying a stage. Num_cluster is the one parameter whose sweep would have made this row C-d = YES by the same route as SHARE, zPROBE, G2uardFL and FedZZ; it is passed into Algorithm 2 as an input and never varied. That four coded papers reach C-d through exactly this knob and BRFL, which has the same knob, does not sweep it, is the sharpest illustration in the frame that the identifying contrast is incidental in this literature rather than sought.

C-e = YES ON THE CRITERION'S FIRST CLAUSE, "asserts why the combination works". The quotation joins the mechanism (validate the cluster averages, take the more accurate cluster) to the outcome (accuracy holds up under a high malicious fraction) in one sentence, and the paper's experiments then set that fraction to 50%, which is exactly the assumption §I says all three prior families require. This is not the AFA pattern that coded C-e = NO: AFA asserted good detection and asserted robustness without ever joining them. Here the join is explicit and it is the paper's own contribution 3.

NOTE ON THE PAPER'S OWN NAME, because the shipped table must not look like a transcription error: the title and body use BRFL, and the abstract twice writes BRLF ("proposes the Blockchainbased Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning (BRLF) model"). Both strings refer to this model. The table uses BRFL.

EXTRACTOR NOTE: the C-c bucket returned ZERO candidates over 71071 characters and the C-d bucket returned one irrelevant candidate, because this paper reports plain accuracy under untargeted attacks and never uses ASR or backdoor vocabulary -- the same aid failure already recorded for BROADCAST and DP-BREM.
